summary: Teach the carbon cycle (ages 12–13) so pupils trace a single carbon atom through photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition and combustion, and reason about the BALANCE OF FLUXES: natural removal (photosynthesis) and return (respiration/decomposition) roughly balance, while humans tip the budget — burning fossil fuels adds long-stored carbon to the air and deforestation reduces the forests that remove it, so atmospheric CO₂ rises and drives climate change. The load-bearing insight is that carbon has always cycled and is conserved — what changed is the rate at which humans unlock stored carbon and cut the forests that take it back. Activities span a manipulable flux model, a tagged diagram, assessment of adds/removes reasoning, and an explanatory extension dialogue.
misconceptions: Thinking carbon is 'used up' or created, rather than conserved and cycled between reservoirs.
Believing plants only add oxygen and animals only add CO₂, missing that plants also respire and that respiration/combustion/decomposition all return CO₂.
Assuming rising atmospheric CO₂ means carbon is newly appearing, rather than being moved rapidly from fossil stores into the air faster than it is removed.
Treating photosynthesis and respiration as unrelated to a global cycle, not seeing them as the balancing biological fluxes.

activities.title: Follow one carbon atom and watch the CO₂ budget
steps: Trace a single carbon atom along its journey: drawn out of the air into a leaf by photosynthesis, eaten along a food chain (feeding), and breathed back out as CO₂ by respiration. Then follow it on a second trip: taken up again by a tree's photosynthesis, locked into wood that dies and is buried before decomposers can fully break it down, slowly turned into coal over millions of years (fossilisation), and finally released as CO₂ when the coal is burned (combustion). Note that if the dead wood had decomposed instead, the decomposers' respiration would have returned the carbon to the air much sooner.
Watch an atmospheric-CO₂ meter while only natural processes run, and state whether removal and return are roughly in balance.
Switch on fossil-fuel burning and deforestation, observe what the meter does, and write down what is actually changing (the rate of addition versus removal, not carbon appearing from nowhere).
Try to steady the meter by dialling emissions down and replanting forests, then explain what each lever does to the budget (replanting restores removal; cutting emissions reduces addition).

Tag each process with whether it ADDS atmospheric CO₂ (respiration, decomposition, combustion), REMOVES it (photosynthesis), or only moves carbon between stores without directly changing atmospheric CO₂ (feeding, fossilisation), and sort them into these groups.
activities.insight: Carbon is conserved and recirculated through reservoirs (atmosphere, living things, fossil fuels); the climate problem is not that carbon moves but that humans add it to the air faster than natural processes (mainly photosynthesis in this model) remove it, tipping a budget that was roughly balanced before.

activities.title: Build and tag the carbon-cycle diagram
steps: Draw or label a carbon-cycle diagram showing photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition and combustion between the reservoirs atmosphere, living things, and fossil fuels.
Arrow each process in its direction and tag it +CO₂ (adds to air), −CO₂ (removes from air), or 0 (moves carbon between other stores, e.g. feeding between living things).
Add a human-activity layer (fossil-fuel burning, deforestation) and mark how it changes the arrows or the balance.
Lift a flap or annotate photosynthesis and combustion to write the matter transformation each performs.
activities.insight: The canonical cycle diagram, with each process tagged by direction, is the representation pupils reason with; it establishes the processes and their +/− effect on atmospheric CO₂ before analysing the dynamic balance.

activities.title: Check adds-vs-removes reasoning and why CO₂ is rising
steps: Categorise each process as adds-CO₂, removes-CO₂, or neither (moves carbon between other stores, e.g. feeding).
Sequence a carbon atom's path through the processes.
Match each process to the reservoir it moves carbon between.
Answer 'why is atmospheric CO₂ rising?' and justify the answer in terms of additions outpacing removals, not carbon being created.
activities.insight: Pupils can confirm the model and, crucially, articulate the flux-balance reason for rising CO₂ rather than reciting that carbon 'increases'.

activities.title: Explain: carbon has always cycled — so what changed?
steps: Respond to the diagnostic: 'A giant oak tree weighs several tonnes. Where did most of that material — the wood, and the carbon in it — actually come from: the soil, or somewhere else? Explain how the carbon got into the tree, and then how that same carbon can end up back in the air.'

Answer probing follow-ups: Van Helmont grew a willow for five years; it gained about 74 kg while the soil lost only about 57 g — where did the extra mass come from? Do plants respire as well as photosynthesise, and what does that mean for carbon? Coal is 'buried sunshine' — trace its carbon back to where it first came from. Name three different ways the carbon locked in that oak could return to the atmosphere.

State explicitly what has changed under human activity: not that carbon moves at all, but that burning fossil fuels unlocks long-stored carbon into the air, while deforestation removes the forests that would take CO₂ back — so additions now outpace removals.
activities.insight: Full mastery: the tree's carbon came from atmospheric CO₂ via photosynthesis, returns via respiration (including the plant's own), combustion and decomposition, carbon is conserved, and human disruption is a change of rate that tips a balanced budget.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A giant oak tree weighs several tonnes. Where did most of that material — the wood, and the carbon in it — actually come from: the soil, or somewhere else? Explain how the carbon got into the tree, and then how that same carbon can end up back in the air.'
checkAnswer: Most of the tree's material and carbon came from carbon dioxide in the AIR, not the soil — captured by photosynthesis and built into glucose and then wood. That carbon returns to the air as CO2 through respiration (of the tree itself, of animals that eat it, and of decomposers), through combustion if the wood burns, and through decomposition when it dies. Carbon cycles — it is not used up.
